The Roll‑Pole

A low-cost, freestanding camera-trap mount for monitoring elephants in active crop fields.

Kuiburi National Park · Thailand 40 cameras 325 nights 0 damaged by elephants
SCROLL
Fundamentals

What is a camera trap?

A camera trap is a camera that takes its own pictures. A passive infrared (PIR) sensor watches for two things at once: heat and movement. When a warm body crosses the sensor's field, the camera fires, day or night, with nobody present.

Ecologists use them to inventory species, estimate populations, record behavior, and document conflict between people and wildlife. They are now among the most widely used tools in wildlife field research.

In an open crop field, almost none of those advantages hold.

?Knowledge check
What two signals does a PIR sensor need before it will trigger?

Heat and motion, together: a warm animal moving across the sensor's field. That pairing is also the weakness. On a hot, open field near 38°C, the background sits close to an elephant's body temperature, so the heat contrast the sensor depends on shrinks and detections can be missed.

The problem

Why open fields are difficult to monitor

Most human-elephant conflict occurs inside active farms, often hundreds of meters from the nearest tree, where elephants enter at night to feed, not at the forest edge. Recording it there requires solving six problems at once.

01🌳

Nothing to mount on

No trees, no posts. The camera has to stand entirely on its own.

02🔥

Extreme heat

Fields run 32–38°C year-round and pass 42°C in the dry season. Sealed metal boxes cook the electronics inside.

03🌧️

Monsoon rain

Half the year is wet. Water kills sensors and corrodes contacts.

04🐘

Elephants

A wild elephant can flatten equipment out of plain curiosity (Varma et al. 2007).

05👀

Theft

Open farmland is accessible, and visible equipment is vulnerable to theft.

06🚜

Farming comes first

Tractors, irrigation, and harvest cannot work around fragile gear.

These six constraints defined the design requirements for the system.

Context

Human-elephant conflict in Thailand

Thailand's wild elephant population has increased over the past decade, and its overlap with farmland has increased with it. In 2023, human-elephant conflict in Thailand killed 22 people, injured 29, and killed 10 elephants (Supanta et al. 2025).

Most damage occurs inside crop fields at night, away from the forest-edge cameras researchers typically rely on (Perera 2009). Managing the conflict requires recording it where it occurs.

Ruam Thai Village sits on the eastern edge of Kuiburi National Park: about 20 km² of farms and 738 households, beside a park holding more than 300 elephants across 969 km².

Conflict in practice: park rangers move an elephant off farmland at night, filmed on a night-vision camera. This is the kind of event the roll-pole is built to record from a fixed position in the field, with no one present.
The system

The roll-pole system

The system is deliberately low-tech: a 3-meter steel pipe set in a concrete-filled car tire, carrying the camera, a sunshade, and a solar panel along its length. Parts cost $50–70. Select each marked part to see the problem it addresses.

Five components

Each component addresses one of the field constraints described earlier. Select the markers on the diagram to explore.

?Knowledge check
Why mount the camera at 1.5 m instead of higher up the pole?

It is the compromise height. 1.5 m sits above the crop canopy and most trunk-reach damage, but low enough to frame the whole animal square-on so you can read body, tusks, and behavior. The team tested 1.8 m too and chose 1.5 m.

Cost

Construction cost and time

Every component comes from a hardware store or salvage yard, and a team of two can build several units at once while the concrete cures (24–48 hours).

🔩Steel pipe, 3 mHardware store$15–20
🛞Automobile tireSalvage$0–5
🧱Concrete, one bagHardware store$10–15
🔗Cable, locks, bracketsHardware store$20–30
⛱️UmbrellaGeneral market$5–10
✅Per roll-pole unit$50–70

The camera mounted on top costs more than the entire mount ($150–400); the roll-pole's purpose is to protect that investment.

Methods

Study design and deployment

From 27 January to 18 December 2023, the team deployed 40 cameras on 20 roll-poles across 20 farms adjacent to the park. Cameras operated nightly from 19:00 to 05:00, the window farmers identified as peak raiding time. SD cards were retrieved every two weeks, and images were processed through Wildlife Insights (an AI identification platform) and then verified by hand.

!A note on units
"325 study nights" is the length of the study, not the total camera effort.

Forty cameras running for 325 nights is closer to 13,000 camera-nights of effort. A study night counts the calendar; a camera-night counts the sampling. Knowing which one a paper reports keeps you from over- or under-stating how much was actually surveyed.

Camera placement

The two-camera configuration

Each pole carried two cameras set diagonally 20–25 m apart with overlapping fields of view, recording the same animal from two angles. In several events, one camera recorded a single elephant while the second showed additional individuals feeding nearby; a single camera would have logged one elephant and missed the group.

Camera 1. One elephant in frame.
Camera 2, same event. A second elephant a single camera would have missed.

The geometry: two cameras per pole, set diagonally 20–25 m apart so their detection zones overlap across the same crop rows.

?Knowledge check
What did the second camera add that one camera could not?

Group size and composition. Overlapping angles catch animals that a single frame hides behind vegetation or another body, which changes how you count a "visit" and how you read social structure.

Results · Equipment durability
0

roll-poles displaced and zero cameras damaged by elephants over 11 months.

Elephants investigated the poles but did not displace or damage them. An earlier prototype with a different base was damaged during pilot trials, which is part of why the 79 kg base, steel construction, and low camera height matter. The only failures were three SD cards, replaced during routine visits.

Results · Detections

What the cameras recorded

The cameras recorded 132 wildlife events: 113 elephants, plus 19 gaur (Bos gaurus), a large wild ox. 16 of the 20 farms recorded wildlife, at a rate of 0.35 elephant events per study night. The paper sets that next to a forest-edge study (0.28 events per trap-night; Varma et al. 2007), but the comparison is worth pausing on: a study night here pools all 40 cameras, while a trap-night is one camera, so the two rates are not measuring the same thing.

Results · Timing

When elephants were detected

Plotting every elephant event reveals two patterns. By hour, detections show two peaks rather than one. By month, they increase during the monsoon. Use the toggle to switch views, and hover any bar for its count.

Two peaks: a first wave at 21:00–23:00, a second at 02:00–04:00. Cameras ran only 19:00–05:00, so daytime visits went unrecorded.
Results · Crop type

Detections by crop type

Grouped by crop, the elephant events show a clear preference. Pineapple recorded the most detections, followed by rubber. Lemongrass, citronella, and galangal, crops grown partly to test whether their odor deters elephants, recorded fewer (Gross et al. 2017). All six crop types recorded activity, which matters methodologically: the same mount functioned across very different field structures and canopy heights.

Elephant events by crop type (n = 113). Hover for counts.

An elephant feeding in galangal, one of the crops grown to test whether its scent deters foraging. Fewer detections does not mean none: the deterrent effect is partial, which is what makes it worth measuring.
?Knowledge check
Why might lemongrass and citronella fields show fewer elephant events?

Two explanations are hard to separate here. Those crops may genuinely repel elephants (an antifeedant smell), or elephants may simply prefer pineapple and rubber and visit them more for unrelated reasons. A camera-trap count shows the pattern; it cannot, on its own, prove the cause. Field data rarely isolates one variable.

Community

Working with farmers

The study depended on the participation of local farmers. All 20 hosted poles for the full 11 months, recruited through the NGO Bring The Elephant Home, and all 20 agreed to host cameras again. Every two weeks, the team walked the fields with them, and farmers indicated where elephants entered and what they damaged.

The cameras didn't get in the way of farm work, and I am interested to see what more you can learn about the elephants. Participating farmer, exit interview

Farmers identified uses the researchers had not prioritized: photographic evidence of damage for compensation claims, and a potential early-warning function from the cellular cameras when elephants leave the park.

⚖Ethics in the field
12 of the 20 farmers raised privacy concerns about night photography.

Images of people were deleted without review, and cameras were positioned away from homes and paths (Sandbrook et al. 2021). The implication for fieldwork: establish data-handling protocols before deployment, not after the first complaint.

Discussion

Limitations

A good methods paper states its limitations directly. Four apply here.

  • Access. The 79 kg base needs a vehicle to deploy. Every site here sat within 50 m of a farm road; more remote sites would not.
  • No control. The team ran no head-to-head trial against other mounts, so "it survived" is not the same as "it outlasts design X."
  • Tame elephants. Kuiburi's elephants are heavily managed and used to people, and may treat strange objects differently than wilder populations would (Jacobson et al. 2023).
  • Placement bias. Four farms recorded nothing at all, indicating that camera placement shapes what is recorded.

Stating these does not weaken the method; it identifies where the next study should test it.

Application

Adapting the design

The specific build is designed for elephants in Thai crop fields, but three design principles apply wherever a camera must be mounted in the open:

⚓

Weighted, freestanding base

Ballast instead of a fixed post: stable, but still movable between seasons. Sand for smaller animals, concrete for big ones.

☂️

Weather shielding

Shed heat and rain without sealing in heat. Match the housing to the harshest day on your site, not the average one.

🔒

Built-in security

Security designed into the structure, not added afterward. A cable routed inside the pole is harder to defeat than an external padlock.

The system is most appropriate when:

  • monitoring has to happen within active fields, not just at forest edges;
  • the target species is large enough to damage a lightweight mount;
  • you need to move gear between crop seasons;
  • budget and materials are local and limited;
  • community trust in the equipment is part of the research.
★Your turn
Name one species and one site you might work on. Which of the three principles, ballast, shielding, or built-in security, would be hardest to meet there?

Whichever principle is hardest at your site is where the design actually begins. A windy ridge stresses ballast; a rainforest stresses shielding; a roadside stresses security. Find the binding constraint first, then build outward from it.

Summary

Monitoring human-elephant conflict means recording it where it occurs: inside active fields, with the farmers who work them.
